question.problem:
Find ${e}^{At}$ for $A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ -2 & 5\end{aligned}].$ *Hint: The only eigenvalue of $A$ is $3,$ and it has multiplicity two.*
${e}^{At}={e}^{3t}\,\,$ {{field-1}} $2t$
{{field-2}} $2t+1$
question.worked_solution:
We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ -2 & 5\end{aligned}]t+{\alpha }_{0}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & 2{\alpha }_{1}t \\ -2{\alpha }_{1}t & 5{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are functions to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The only eigenvalue or $At$ is 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=3t
$$

of multiplicity two. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}r(3t)={e}^{3t} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\lambda }r(3t)={e}^{3t}\end{aligned}\,⇒\,\{\begin{aligned}3t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{3t} \\ {\alpha }_{1}={e}^{3t}\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

- From the second equation, we get

$$
{\alpha }_{1}={e}^{3t}.
$$

- Substituting this into the first one, we get

$$
3t{e}^{3t}+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{3t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{3t}(1-3t).
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the required entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & ={e}^{3t}t+{e}^{3t}(1-3t) \\  & ={e}^{3t}(1-2t) \\ -2{\alpha }_{1}t & =-2{e}^{3t}t \\  & ={e}^{3t}(-2t)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{e}^{At}={e}^{3t}[\begin{aligned}1-2t & 2t \\ -2t & 2t+1\end{aligned}].
$$
